cards.front: Perplexity is useful when—and limited when?
cards.back: Useful for model/data comparison on language modeling; limited for open-ended apps where human goals aren’t captured by next-token likelihood.
Non-negotiable gates: does the output run/work (SQL executes, code passes tests) before softer quality signals.
Position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference, inconsistency—needs calibration and human spot checks.
Relative human preference between models—complements but doesn’t replace absolute thresholds (pass rate, latency, cost).
Exact/functional checks → scalable AI judges/semantic metrics → human review on high-stakes or ambiguous cases.
Test data may appear in training—public leaderboard gains may not transfer to your distribution.

questions.prompt: Low perplexity on a holdout set implies for your chatbot:
choices: Better LM fit to that distribution—not necessarily task success
questions.explanation: LM metrics don’t fully encode instruction-following or business outcomes.

questions.prompt: For text-to-SQL, the first eval gate should be:
choices: Does the SQL run and return correct results?
questions.explanation: Synthesis example: functional correctness before judges or humans.

choices: As the only signal, never audited
At scale with known biases and human sanity checks
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 documents judge failure modes and mitigation.

questions.prompt: Winning on a public Arena leaderboard means:
choices: Relative preference signal—you still need absolute bars for production
questions.explanation: Pair comparative ranking with pass rates, latency, and cost.

questions.prompt: Open-ended outputs are hard to benchmark because:
choices: Many valid answers exist; static labels under-specify quality
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 motivates exact, judge, and comparative methods together.
